question: Was it mocking the scholars to trace the 48-mile travel distance to Queen Elizabeth I?
answer:
Okay, I said I'm going to do one other thing, and then we're done, inshallah. And that other thing is as follows. From last week, somebody pointed out to me a long semi-article somebody wrote, that they really did not like the fact that I mentioned Queen Elizabeth I. They were very irritated, and they said that I am trying to make fun — a'udhu billah — of the scholars of Islam. A'udhu billah, I have never wanted to do this. But I'm simply teaching you where these measures came from. And so there was this issue of, I'm trying to be mocking when I mention Queen Elizabeth and whatnot.

You know, one of my mentors said to me: any time somebody criticizes you, before you become defensive, think: maybe there's an element of truth. And then also understand the psychology of the critic. And in this case, I really don't think I have done anything wrong by telling you a factually correct statement: that the person, or the entity, or the group that defined the mile the way that we understand it is Queen Elizabeth I's era. She got together a group and they passed a law.

And just to prove this point — and by the way, the whole issue of how many miles, as we said, there's so many opinions, this, this, this many. Suppose we say it is 48 miles. Suppose we say that, even though from the Prophet ﷺ, if anything, some things are mentioned in burud and farsakh. Suppose we say 48 miles. I actually wanted to explain to you what this is.

For example, Hajjawi, one of the great scholars of Hanbali Islam — listen to this — he says: a mile is 12,000 steps. Every step is 6,000 dhira'. Every dhira' is 24 fingers in length, width-wise. Each finger is six grains of barley, if you lay them side by side. Each grain of barley is the size of six hairs from a workhorse called a birdhawn. This is how he is defining it. It's not Queen Elizabeth I. And some modern people have tried to calculate this out, and they have gotten varying numbers, from 80 to 160. Because what is a hand, a dhira'? What is a finger? If you have a 0.1 inch difference in a finger, by the time you get to how many fingers are in that, the answer is going to be much larger. So the variation is so large.

Ibn al-Rif'ah, who was the one put in charge in 7th-century Cairo of the marketplace, hisba and measurements, wrote a book, a chronicle of weights and measurements, and he called it al-Idah wal-Bayan fi Ma'rifat al-Mikyal wal-Mizan. And he writes in this book that our scholars have differed on how much a mile is. The Hanafiyyah said it is 4,000 — this is dhira' — 4,000 dhira'. The Malikiyyah, some of them, like Ibn Abd al-Barr, said it is 3,500. And Ibn Habib said that it is 2,000. And al-Dasuqi said the famous position of the Malikis is that it is 2,000, and some have said it is 3,500. The Shafi'iyyah said the mile is 4,000 steps. The Hanabilah said the mile is 6,000 dhira'. And this is how much they defined it. Now, even within — this is a classical book.

And I wanted to explain: I'm not making fun of anyone. I'm just saying — and I'm sorry if this offends you — but it is a factually correct statement. If you feel that when you are driving your car — that's what I said, driving your car, I explicitly said that — and when you cross 48 miles on your car odometer — I know exactly what I said — you think that your safar has begun: the car odometer is 48 miles. Who said that's 48? Ibn Qudamah? Al-Dasuqi? Al-Nawawi? Ibn Hajar? Where'd you get that from? And I'm sorry to be breaking the news to you: that definition comes from Queen Elizabeth I. Your car odometer was not measured by a classical scholar of Islam. And even in the classical scholars, I just gave you seven positions about how much a mile is. And by the way, even the 48 number is a huge controversy: how many burud, how many farasikh, the conversion factors — it is so much.

And so this really does go back to this issue: the reason why I brought this topic was so that we appreciate, in a very non-emotional topic... At the end of the day, who cares if you follow the 48 position? It's not a big deal. I wanted to bring a topic that has no emotion. Why? Because there are topics that are emotionally charged: gender issues and roles, societal issues, democracy, living in the secular state. These are much more — people think they know the haqq immediately, and they might quote you a classical position about a modern issue. And I purposely wanted to demonstrate: guys, we respect our 'ulama immensely, but they're human beings. Had I been alive a thousand years ago, I would be the same thing. **Just because many 'ulama said 48 miles doesn't make it the religion of Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala.**

Now, what does that mean? Free for all? No. The other group, that want to stick with the madhhabs — I respect them. They are looking at what happened, especially in the 80s and 90s, when a certain trend arose and they opened the door for a free-for-all. And this free-for-all led to a lot of chaos in the Ummah, and splintering and deviation. And some have even said that radicalism and these fundamentalist movements are a result — even though that's not fully true, but perhaps there's an element of truth. Perhaps there's an element of truth, because at the end of the day, those movements do stem from the larger movement that did open this door. But I don't think that is the main reason. But they see what happened from opening the door for ijtihad.

So this has resulted in a new generation coming — and it's human nature, for every action there's an equal and opposite reaction — a new generation, much more nuanced, much more, alhamdulillah, educated than the 80s and 90s generation, and they're saying, we're going to stick with it; let's not open this door at all. And I appreciate the sentiment. But if we want Islam to flourish, for the more difficult questions... Safar is no big deal. You want to stick to 48? Alhamdulillah. But I purposely went into two hours of lectures to demonstrate the evolution of fiqh in a case study. I did it on purpose, so that we then have an idea.

Now, does this mean all of us in this audience are going to do this? No. Obviously, our 'ulama do it. And here we go to the final point. My suggestion to all of you: it is up to you. You choose the 'alim or the 'ulama that you think are the most suited. You have to; that's your ijtihad. And there are plenty, and 'ulama have track records.

And I personally look up to a group of 'ulama across the world, and especially the councils of fiqh. I really look up to them, and generally speaking I'm sympathetic to that strand of fiqh which is respectful of the madhhabs, but not blind following them. This is my version, that we really respect. And generally I do follow the Hanbali madhhab in my personal life, and I follow that. But in some issues, especially in issues that are going to be controversial to the Muslims of our times, difficult for them as a society to follow, we have to rethink through, and that's where fiqh councils come in handy.

You have many great 'ulama: Shaykh Qaradawi is there, Shaykh Yusuf al-Judda; I look up to Shaykh Salman al-Awdah, Shaykh Muhammad al-Hasan al-Dadew. And these are all, within their own way, slightly different; they're not all the same. But all of them are on the same wavelength: we come from the madhhabs with respect, but we fine-tune where needed. These are the groups I look up to. Overall, the fatwas I give you generally will come from that school of modern Islamic thought, and I respect that.

Some people find this uncomfortable, and they want to stick completely. That's fine; Allah is not going to punish you. Go for it. But I firmly believe, if we want our children and their grandchildren to really practice Islam and flourish, we're going to have to rethink through some issues. Not safar — safar is not a big deal — but just to give you a case study.
